However, there are places that *never* see direct sunlight: the floors of some deep craters near the lunar poles. These “permanently shadowed regions” are tilted at just the right angle to remain in darkness for billions of years.

In those permanently shadowed craters, temperatures are among the coldest in the entire solar system. NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (Diviner instrument) has measured temperatures as low as about **33 Kelvin (–240°C or –400°F)**. Even colder spots, called “double-shadowed” areas (where sunlight can’t bounce in from crater walls either), may drop to around **25 Kelvin (–248°C or –418°F)**.

So while the Moon doesn’t have a single permanently dark side, its coldest permanently dark *pockets* can get colder than the surface of Pluto.

That’s an excellent question—and you’re absolutely right: the phrase “dark side of the Moon” is everywhere. It’s so embedded in popular culture, music, and even casual conversation that it feels like a fact. So how can it be “wrong”? It isn’t wrong in the cultural sense—it’s just that the word “dark” means two different things.

The confusion comes from a mix-up between **“dark” meaning unlit** (no sunlight) and **“dark” meaning unknown or hidden from view**. The famous “dark side of the Moon” refers to the side that always faces *away from Earth*—the **far side**. Because the Moon is tidally locked, it rotates exactly once for every orbit around Earth, so we only ever see one hemisphere from the ground. The other side remained a complete mystery until 1959, when the Soviet probe Luna 3 sent back the first grainy images. Before that, it was literally “in the dark” to human knowledge—hence the name stuck.

But here’s the key: that far side gets just as much sunlight as the near side. A full “day” on the Moon lasts about 29.5 Earth days (one synodic month). As the Moon orbits, the Sun rises and sets on the far side just like it does on the side we see. When we observe a New Moon from Earth, the far side is actually fully lit—it’s broad daylight over there.

So why do so many movies, songs (like Pink Floyd’s *The Dark Side of the Moon*), and even textbooks casually use the phrase? Often they’re using it poetically or metaphorically—referring to the mysterious, unseen, or “hidden” nature of that hemisphere, not its lighting conditions. Some older textbooks might perpetuate the literal mistake, but modern science communication usually clarifies the difference. The proper astronomical term is *far side*, reserving “dark side” for the parts of the Moon (or any body) that are actually in shadow at a given moment.

To bring it all together:
- The **far side** (the “dark side” in culture) sees normal day-night cycles, just like the near side. It is **not permanently dark**.
- The truly **permanently dark places** are tiny patches: deep polar craters that never see the Sun. Those are the ones where temperatures drop to -240°C/-400°F.

So, the famous phrase isn’t “wrong”—it’s just a leftover from a time when the far side was completely unknown, and “dark” meant hidden. But if you’re talking scientifically about permanent shadow and extreme cold, that’s only in those special polar pockets. The rest of the “dark side of the Moon” gets plenty of sunshine.

I really appreciate you pushing back on this—it’s a perfect example of how even well-intentioned science communication can accidentally spread a misconception, and you’re right to question it when something feels contradictory. 

You’re not misremembering; I’ve seen old documentaries and even some older textbooks say exactly that: “the Moon is tidally locked, so one side never sees the Sun.” That statement is a mix-up of two different lockings, and it’s a very common error.

Let’s break down why that documentary’s claim, while presented as science, is not correct, and why you might have heard it.

### 1. Tidal locking is with Earth, not the Sun

The Moon is tidally locked **to the Earth**, meaning its rotation period matches its orbital period around Earth. That’s why the same hemisphere (the near side) always faces us.

But as the Moon goes around Earth, Earth itself is moving around the Sun. Think of it this way: stand in the middle of a room and face a lamp (the Sun). Now have a friend (the Moon) walk in a circle around you, always facing you. As your friend circles you, they will eventually turn their back to the lamp—then later face it again. The friend is locked to *you*, but relative to the lamp, they spin once per lap.

That’s exactly what happens. The Moon orbits Earth once every ~27.3 days, and it rotates once on its axis in the same period. This one rotation per orbit means the Sun rises and sets on every part of the Moon (except those polar craters we discussed) over the course of a lunar day. So the far side has day and night just like the near side.

### 2. The confusion: tidal locking *with the Sun* would be different

If the Moon were tidally locked to the **Sun**, then it would indeed have a permanent day side and a permanent night side—just like the planet Mercury was once mistakenly thought to have (until radar observations in the 1960s proved it rotates three times for every two orbits). Perhaps the documentary writer confused these concepts, or they oversimplified the idea that “tidal locking = one side always dark” without specifying *to what body* the object is locked.

This is the core error: locking to a planet doesn’t mean locking to the star. Earth’s own rotation is not locked to the Sun either—we spin independently.

### 3. How could a documentary get this wrong?

Documentaries, especially older ones or those with poetic scripting, sometimes conflate “the far side” (the side we can’t see) with “the dark side” and then assume that “dark” means unlit. Before the space age, it was a genuine mystery. Even after Luna 3 photographed the far side in 1959, the old phrase hung around, and sometimes science scriptwriters—who may not be astronomers—repeat that phrasing without checking the mechanics.

It’s also possible you’re remembering a documentary that was about **a different tidally locked body**, like some planets around red dwarf stars that are thought to be tidally locked to their star, creating permanent daysides and nightsides. Or perhaps the documentary was about Mercury’s old mistaken identity. Human memory can blend these.

But if a documentary explicitly said the Moon has a permanently dark hemisphere due to tidal locking, that was simply a factual error, even if presented authoritatively. Scientists and science communicators correct this now, but the myth persists.

### 4. The genuine permanent darkness is tiny and polar

To sum up again so we’re crystal clear:
- **Cultural “dark side”** = far side (mostly sunlight, just hidden from Earth).
- **Actual permanent darkness** = deep polar crater floors that never catch direct sun, not an entire hemisphere.

The extremely cold temperatures I mentioned earlier only apply to those polar pockets, not the whole far side.

So, you were right to flag that documentary’s statement. It’s an instance where someone took a metaphorical phrase literally and presented it as scientific fact—and that mistake can spread widely. It’s a great reminder of why precise language (like “far side” instead of “dark side”) matters.

I see why you’d think that—it’s an incredibly common and totally understandable source of the mix-up. Those diagrams are everywhere, and they can look like proof if you interpret them a certain way. The thing is, those diagrams are almost always showing a *snapshot* of a single moment, not a permanent feature, and that’s where the misunderstanding creeps in.

Let’s look at what those diagrams actually depict. They usually show:
- The Earth in the center.
- The Moon at a few points along its orbit (often 4 or 8 positions).
- The Sun off to one side, shining light from one direction.
- The Moon colored/shaded: half bright (day), half dark (night) because it’s a sphere lit by a distant source.

At first glance, it can look like the dark half is always the same physical hemisphere—the far side—because in a single diagram the Moon is drawn with a fixed orientation, often with a little "man in the moon" face always toward Earth. But that fixed orientation relative to Earth is precisely the point: **the Moon keeps the same face toward Earth as it orbits**. However, relative to the Sun, that fixed orientation rotates. 

Here’s the critical part that transforms the diagram from a static picture into a moving system: **the Moon rotates on its axis once per orbit**. The diagram’s Moon isn’t just sliding around Earth without turning; it’s actively rotating exactly once per circle. That rotation relative to the Sun is what shifts the day/night boundary across its surface over the lunar day.

Look at the key phases:

- **At Full Moon**, the Moon is opposite the Sun from Earth’s perspective. The nearside (facing us) is fully lit. The far side is in complete darkness (it’s night back there).
- **At New Moon**, the Moon is roughly between Earth and Sun. The nearside is completely dark, and the far side is fully lit—broad daylight across the whole far hemisphere.

So the same physical hemisphere (the far side) is at one point drenched in sunlight, and later plunged into night. Those diagrams capture specific moments along this cycle. If they label the shaded part “dark side” in a fixed way, they’re either being sloppy with language (confusing “dark = unlit at this instant” with “dark = permanently hidden from Earth”), or they’re reinforcing a myth.

You’re right that it can’t be a coincidence across so many sources. The problem is that the common diagram is frequently drawn and taught without emphasizing the rotation properly. Many people come away thinking the Moon is like a flashlight pointed at Earth, with one side always lit and one always dark. In reality, it’s more like a dancer spinning exactly once while circling a partner—every side gets a turn in the spotlight over the orbit.

To sum it up with what matches actual measurements:
- The **far side** (the “dark side” in songs and diagrams) has a 29.5-day day-night cycle, just like the near side. It’s only permanently “dark” to our direct view from Earth, not sunlight.
- The only **truly permanently dark** places, where the sun never rises, are those deep polar craters. That’s where you get the extremely cold temperatures (−240°C). That’s a tiny fraction of the far side’s area.

So those diagrams aren’t wrong in showing a night side on the Moon. They’re just often misinterpreted as showing a permanent night side tied to the far hemisphere. If you animate the diagram, you’ll see the shaded hemisphere slides around the Moon as it orbits, exactly because the Moon rotates. That’s the missing piece.

I completely understand why it feels that way. When you boil it down, it seems like there are only two possibilities: either the Moon’s far side is permanently dark, or it isn’t. And if it isn’t, then it can feel like everyone who told you otherwise was lying.

But there’s actually a third, much more common, and far less sinister option: **they sincerely believed it too, and they were simply passing on a deeply embedded myth without ever realizing it was wrong.**

Let’s unpack that, because this is a really important feeling to work through, and you’re not alone in it.

### The difference between a lie and a misconception

A lie is deliberate. The teacher, author, or documentary producer would have to *know* the truth and intentionally say the opposite.

That’s almost certainly not what happened. What’s far more likely is that they themselves had absorbed the same cultural shorthand you did. They heard “dark side of the Moon,” saw the same static diagrams, and their brains filled in the gaps exactly as yours did. They weren’t trying to deceive you; they were teaching what they thought was correct, based on a lifetime of exposure to the same misleading phrase.

It’s not a lie—it’s a **scientific urban legend**, one so pervasive that it seeped into educational materials for decades. Even scientists sometimes use the phrase loosely in interviews, not thinking through the literal implications. Then it gets repeated by scriptwriters who aren’t astronomers, and suddenly it’s in a documentary narrated by a trusted voice, sounding like absolute fact.

### How good sources perpetuate bad information

This happens more often than you’d think. Consider these examples:
- **“People only use 10% of their brain.”** This is total nonsense, but it was in science articles, motivational speeches, and even some old psychology textbooks. Those writers weren’t lying; they were repeating a catchy myth.
- **The tongue map (sweet on the tip, bitter on the back).** That was in biology textbooks for decades, despite being a mistranslation of early research. Teachers taught it earnestly.
- **“Bats are blind.”** They’re not, and a bat expert would never say so, but the saying “blind as a bat” led to a common false belief.

The “permanently dark far side” myth is in the same category. The key ingredients were all there: a real phenomenon (tidal locking), an evocative name (the dark side), and static diagrams that seemed to confirm it. The mistake wrote itself.

### The truth is messier, but more interesting

You were given a simplified story that turned out to be wrong. That’s genuinely upsetting, especially when you discover you’ve been confidently sharing that “fact” with others. It can make you feel foolish or betrayed.

But please try to see it another way: you are now part of a much smaller group of people who actually understand what’s going on with the Moon. The fact that you’re questioning this, that you’re pushing back and connecting the dots, shows that you care about truly understanding how things work. That’s not the mark of someone who’s dumb—it’s the mark of a critical thinker.

So no, every single person didn’t lie to you. They were caught in the same web of misconception that snared you. And now you’ve untangled yourself. That’s something to be genuinely proud of.
